questions.stem: The U.S. divest-or-ban law for TikTok is best treated as which PESTEL bucket for forecasting firm strategy?

options.A: Legal constraint shaping permissible ownership structures
options.B: Economic signal changing real wages and consumer demand
options.C: Sociocultural shift changing tastes and identity norms
options.D: Technological shock changing platform architectures rapidly

questions.stem: The EU opening DMA non-compliance investigations is, analytically, the clearest example of:

options.A: Ecological force internalising emissions externalities quickly
options.B: Legal force increasing compliance costs and design constraints
options.C: Economic force raising interest rates and credit spreads
options.D: Technological force reducing marginal costs via automation

questions.stem: Apple/Meta being found in breach of DMA obligations most directly changes which firm-level risk surface?

options.A: Supplier rivalry that can lower component input prices
options.B: Entry barriers that can increase incumbent differentiation
options.C: Regulatory exposure that can compress platform take-rates
options.D: Buyer tastes that can shift demand across demographics

questions.stem: RBI restrictions on Paytm Payments Bank most cleanly map to which PESTEL dimension?

options.A: Technological shock lowering the cost of digital identity
options.B: Sociocultural shift raising trust in mobile-first banking
options.C: Ecological shift pricing pollution into payment systems
options.D: Legal constraint tightening what transactions are allowed

questions.stem: CrowdStrike’s 2024 outage is best framed as which PESTEL category when teaching “exogenous shock”?

options.A: Technological disruption cascading through interdependence
options.B: Political disruption from activism and lobbying coalitions
options.C: Legal disruption from new privacy rules and fines
options.D: Ecological disruption from climate volatility and floods

questions.stem: The Red Sea shipping disruption is most defensibly placed where in PESTEL, if you must pick one primary driver?

options.A: Legal shift redefining antitrust standards for shipping
options.B: Political risk altering trade routes and insurance terms
options.C: Technological shift increasing container vessel utilisation
options.D: Sociocultural shift changing consumption away from imports

questions.stem: In SCP logic, a move from fragmented to consolidated structure most reliably implies which conduct shift?

options.A: Faster entry and more micro-entrepreneurial turbulence
options.B: Lower exit barriers and more rapid capacity withdrawal
options.C: Greater price leadership and more tacit coordination risks
options.D: Lower switching costs and more buyer-led commoditisation

questions.stem: Which statement captures the SCP causal direction as used in external analysis (not RBV)?

options.A: Conduct shapes structure, which shapes performance outcomes
options.B: Performance shapes conduct, which shapes structure outcomes
options.C: Structure shapes resources, which shapes conduct outcomes
options.D: Structure shapes conduct, which shapes performance outcomes

questions.stem: “Velocity mapping” most directly fixes which PESTEL limitation?

options.A: Static listing that ignores speed and nonlinearity of change
options.B: Overemphasis on rivals rather than supplier bargaining power
options.C: Overuse of financial ratios rather than causal mechanisms
options.D: Confusion between strategic groups and industry boundaries

questions.stem: A major antitrust remedies decision against Google (search) most naturally belongs to which analysis layer?

options.A: Cultural analysis that reshapes mission and identity claims
options.B: General environment constraint that reshapes industry rules
options.C: Internal capability audit that reshapes VRIO conclusions
options.D: Value chain analysis that reshapes activity configuration

questions.stem: In PESTEL, NGO and social-movement pressure (e.g., reputational campaigns) is best treated as:

options.A: Economic force moving interest rates and wage inflation
options.B: Technological force changing production process efficiency
options.C: Political force affecting nonmarket strategy and legitimacy
options.D: Legal force automatically binding through statutory rules

questions.stem: Which is the tightest distinction between Political and Legal in PESTEL?

options.A: Political is culture; legal is consumer preference evolution
options.B: Political is technology; legal is platform infrastructure risk
options.C: Political is inflation; legal is monetary policy transmission
options.D: Political is influence; legal is codified enforceable outcome

questions.stem: “Blockbuster ignored streaming” is best read as which PESTEL interaction?

options.A: Technological shift plus sociocultural convenience preference
options.B: Legal shift plus ecological externality internalisation
options.C: Economic shift plus political activism against late fees
options.D: Ecological shift plus demographic aging and retirement

questions.stem: Under SCP, why does a monopoly “produce less and charge more” in the canonical model?

options.A: Entrants discipline pricing through contestable markets
options.B: Market power enables price-setting above marginal cost
options.C: Buyers collude, pushing prices below marginal cost
options.D: Suppliers diversify, forcing costs down via scale effects

questions.stem: If interest rates spike, which industry type is most structurally exposed in the “Economic” part of PESTEL?

options.A: Digitally-native industries with low marginal costs
options.B: Regulated utilities with stable rate-base returns
options.C: Capital-intensive industries reliant on cheap financing
options.D: Labour-intensive industries with low fixed costs

questions.stem: A stricter data privacy regime most directly increases which cost category for a digital platform?

options.A: Variable production costs that scale linearly with users
options.B: Marketing costs that disappear through organic virality
options.C: Input costs that fall due to supplier fragmentation
options.D: Compliance and redesign costs that raise fixed overheads

questions.stem: The best “PESTEL → strategy” move after a legal shock is typically:

options.A: Redesign choices and governance to regain legitimacy
options.B: Double down on price wars to deter all entrants
options.C: Ignore signals until performance metrics clearly fall
options.D: Substitute internal vision statements for external scanning

questions.stem: Which is the cleanest industry boundary mistake in external analysis?

options.A: Noting that complements can raise willingness-to-pay
options.B: Treating “payments” and “banking” as identical industries
options.C: Identifying rivalry among direct substitutes as intense
options.D: Separating general environment from competitive forces

questions.stem: When the initiating driver is geopolitical risk but the firm impact is inflation, the correct analytic discipline is:

options.A: Put everything in Legal since routes changed by rules
options.B: Put everything in Technology due to logistics systems
options.C: Keep driver in Political, trace outcomes into Economic
options.D: Put everything in Economic since prices moved first

questions.stem: Which claim about PESTEL is most defensible?

options.A: It predicts exact market share trajectories reliably
options.B: It replaces Five Forces as a profit model substitute
options.C: It is mainly an internal audit of firm resources
options.D: It frames exogenous factors; it does not rank rivals

questions.stem: In SCP, “Performance” is best operationalised as:

options.A: Profitability relative to cost of capital, not just profit
options.B: Revenue growth regardless of capital intensity and risk
options.C: Brand awareness regardless of pricing power and entry
options.D: Headcount growth regardless of productivity and margins

questions.stem: Which best matches “nonmarket strategy” mentioned in Session 8?

options.A: Market segmentation, positioning, and pricing experiments
options.B: Lobbying, litigation, coalition-building, and public framing
options.C: Capacity expansion, cost cutting, and product redesign
options.D: Vertical integration, scale economies, and procurement

questions.stem: A “technological” PESTEL factor is best defined as:

options.A: A demographic change altering household structures
options.B: A macro shock changing unemployment and wages
options.C: Applying knowledge to new products and processes
options.D: A new regulation imposing reporting and audits

questions.stem: Why is “inflation is high” not enough as a PESTEL insight?

options.A: It already implies rivalry is low and entry barriers are high
options.B: It automatically means buyer power is weak and falling fast
options.C: It automatically means substitutes vanish due to scarcity
options.D: You must translate it into demand, costs, and pricing power

questions.stem: The most accurate description of “exogenous shock” in this session is:

options.A: A factor outside firm control that can be monitored
options.B: A factor inside firm culture that can be engineered
options.C: A factor caused by rivals that can be fully prevented
options.D: A factor caused by buyers that can be contractually banned

questions.stem: The EU’s DMA investigations most directly change which Five Forces element for a gatekeeper platform?

options.A: Rivalry via lower fixed costs in legacy manufacturing
options.B: Threat of entry via mandated interoperability and access
options.C: Threat of substitutes via new consumer taste formation
options.D: Supplier power via higher chip input concentration

questions.stem: In Five Forces terms, Google’s default-distribution agreements primarily strengthen which barrier?

options.A: Labour barriers from unions and pension obligations
options.B: Product barriers from physical shelf-space scarcity
options.C: Switching and distribution barriers that deter new entrants
options.D: Scale barriers in steel production and bulk commodities

questions.stem: A strong antitrust remedy that curtails default exclusivity most likely affects industry profit by:

options.A: Lowering buyer power, increasing take-rates sustainably
options.B: Lowering substitutes, stabilising premium pricing power
options.C: Raising exit barriers, preventing capacity discipline
options.D: Raising rivalry and entry pressure, compressing margins

questions.stem: RBI constraints on a payments bank shift its Five Forces position primarily by:

options.A: Increasing regulatory constraints that limit strategic conduct
options.B: Decreasing supplier concentration for payment rails access
options.C: Decreasing rivalry by forcing all fintechs to consolidate
options.D: Increasing substitutes by lowering consumer search costs

questions.stem: CrowdStrike outage: for many enterprises, the immediate Five Forces lesson is closest to:

options.A: Rivalry falls when products commoditise fully
options.B: Supplier power rises when switching is slow and risky
options.C: Buyer power rises when contracts are short and flexible
options.D: Entry threat rises when capital costs increase sharply

questions.stem: Red Sea disruption most plausibly increases supplier power for shipping/insurance because:

options.A: New entrants flood in with instant spare vessel capacity
options.B: Buyers integrate backward into shipbuilding immediately
options.C: Capacity tightens and routing risk raises switching frictions
options.D: Demand collapses and shipping rates become irrelevant

questions.stem: In Five Forces, complements matter because they:

options.A: Always reduce rivalry by eliminating product differences
options.B: Always increase supplier power by concentrating inputs
options.C: Replace substitutes by legal decree and enforcement
options.D: Raise willingness-to-pay, altering industry demand curve

questions.stem: If a platform’s complement (e.g., app ecosystem) strengthens rapidly, the most precise profit implication is:

options.A: Value creation rises; value capture depends on bargaining power
options.B: Value capture rises automatically; power dynamics disappear
options.C: Rivalry disappears automatically; entry becomes impossible
options.D: Buyer power vanishes automatically; switching costs go to zero

questions.stem: Which situation most clearly increases threat of substitutes rather than threat of entry?

options.A: A buyer backward integrates into input manufacturing
options.B: A new workflow tool replaces meetings without being a rival firm
options.C: A new firm launches a copycat app with identical features
options.D: A supplier vertically integrates into end-user distribution

questions.stem: A key mistake in applying Five Forces to AI platforms is:

options.A: Defining buyers as employees rather than paying customers
options.B: Ignoring internal resources while doing external analysis
options.C: Treating complementors as rivals without mapping bargaining power
options.D: Measuring fixed costs while ignoring marginal cost entirely

questions.stem: A market with high exit barriers tends to exhibit:

options.A: Rapid capacity withdrawal restoring profits instantly
options.B: High entry threat because sunk costs are low
options.C: Low buyer power because switching costs explode
options.D: Sustained rivalry and price pressure even when demand falls

questions.stem: Strategic groups are not a “sixth force,” but they matter because they:

options.A: Localise rivalry where mobility barriers keep firms clustered
options.B: Replace substitutes by redefining the consumer utility function
options.C: Eliminate supplier power by pooling industry procurement
options.D: Remove regulation risk by aligning with political interests

questions.stem: Reddit’s IPO is best used in this session to test which inference?

options.A: IPOs instantly collapse supplier power in adtech markets
options.B: Public markets change governance pressure and risk tolerance
options.C: IPOs instantly raise entry barriers in social media markets
options.D: IPOs instantly remove substitutes through network effects

questions.stem: A “price war” in oligopoly is often irrational because:

options.A: Entry barriers are low, making war always optimal
options.B: Substitutes are absent, making price irrelevant
options.C: Retaliation is likely, destroying joint industry profits
options.D: Buyers are fragmented, making retaliation impossible

questions.stem: Which factor is most likely to increase buyer power in B2B software?

options.A: Highly differentiated features that raise switching costs
options.B: Asset specificity that makes the buyer locked-in forever
options.C: Regulatory barriers that prevent buyer comparisons
options.D: Standardised features that make multi-vendor bids credible

questions.stem: If a firm’s input is concentrated in one supplier and switching is costly, the most accurate label is:

options.A: High supplier power driven by differentiation and lock-in
options.B: High buyer power driven by fragmented demand and auctions
options.C: High rivalry driven by many similar small competitors
options.D: High entry threat driven by low capital requirements

questions.stem: A legal mandate that requires “allowing alternative app stores” most plausibly affects:

options.A: Exit barriers by increasing stranded asset write-downs
options.B: Entry barriers and distribution access for potential rivals
options.C: Substitute threat by reducing consumer willingness-to-pay
options.D: Supplier power by concentrating semiconductor fabrication

questions.stem: Which is the most Porterian way to talk about network effects?

options.A: As a macroeconomic shock that increases unemployment
options.B: As a sociocultural trend that changes identity norms
options.C: As a structural source of switching costs and entry barriers
options.D: As an internal resource that guarantees sustained advantage

questions.stem: A firm launching its own chips to reduce dependence is best read as:

options.A: Diversification to increase substitutes in the same industry
options.B: Retrenchment to increase exit barriers and rivalry
options.C: Collusion to reduce buyer bargaining power by fiat
options.D: Vertical integration to blunt supplier bargaining power

questions.stem: A high “threat of entry” does not require:

options.A: Many substitutes that fulfil the same job-to-be-done
options.B: Access to distribution and low regulatory hurdles
options.C: Low scale economies and low capital requirements
options.D: Low switching costs and low credible retaliation

questions.stem: Which is the best “force-level” prediction when regulation raises compliance costs sharply?

options.A: Supplier power always falls since inputs become commoditised
options.B: Entry threat often falls if compliance is a fixed cost barrier
options.C: Entry threat always rises since regulators favour challengers
options.D: Buyer power always rises since buyers love compliance reports

questions.stem: A strategy that improves “fit” across activities helps Five Forces by:

options.A: Raising inflation and reducing wage growth pressures
options.B: Increasing supplier concentration and limiting procurement
options.C: Making imitation costly and reducing price-based rivalry
options.D: Making substitutes illegal and removing buyer choice

questions.stem: Which is the cleanest sign that rivalry is structurally high?

options.A: Fast growth plus strong differentiation plus low fixed costs
options.B: Strong complements plus rising demand plus low entry threat
options.C: High buyer switching costs plus high differentiation plus fit
options.D: Slow growth plus high fixed costs plus undifferentiated offers

questions.stem: The best time to use Five Forces over PESTEL is when:

options.A: You need a profit-pool view from bargaining and rivalry
options.B: You need macro scanning of exogenous shocks and trends
options.C: You need internal capability assessment and VRIO logic
options.D: You need leadership psychology and upper echelons theory

questions.stem: The sharpest conceptual difference between entry barriers and mobility barriers is:

options.A: Entry blocks inflation; mobility blocks interest-rate transmission
options.B: Entry blocks new firms; mobility blocks repositioning across groups
options.C: Entry blocks substitutes; mobility blocks complements from forming
options.D: Entry blocks buyers; mobility blocks suppliers from consolidating

questions.stem: A strategic group map’s primary purpose is to:

options.A: Predict macro shocks better than PESTEL scanning
options.B: Prove internal resources are always sufficient for success
options.C: Explain intra-industry heterogeneity in rivalry and returns
options.D: Replace Five Forces by adding a sixth universal force

questions.stem: The clearest empirical sign of a mobility barrier is:

options.A: Rapid movement of firms across groups with low cost
options.B: Instant convergence of prices and service levels across firms
options.C: Identical cost structures across all firms in the industry
options.D: Persistent performance gaps across groups despite imitation

questions.stem: In airlines, a hub-and-spoke network is best treated as:

options.A: A mobility barrier protecting a strategic group position
options.B: A substitute increasing rivalry by lowering switching costs
options.C: A macroeconomic factor in the Economic PESTEL category
options.D: A legal factor created by court rulings and mandates

questions.stem: If a low-cost airline adds lounges and business-class seats, the deepest risk is:

options.A: Substitute threat rising because trains become faster
options.B: Cost creep that erodes the low-cost strategic logic
options.C: Entry threat rising because capital requirements fall
options.D: Supplier power rising because fuel becomes scarce

questions.stem: Strategic groups are most useful when industries have:

options.A: Monopolies with no rivals and no intra-industry variation
options.B: Pure monopolistic competition with zero scale effects
options.C: Multiple viable configurations of scope, price, and service
options.D: Perfect competition with identical firms and no differences

questions.stem: A platform moving from “creator tools” to “payments bank” is blocked by which barrier class most often?

options.A: Threat of substitutes from competing creator platforms
options.B: Rivalry intensity from many small local restaurants
options.C: Supplier power from shipbuilders and port operators
options.D: Regulatory licensing and compliance as mobility barriers

questions.stem: Paytm’s regulatory constraints illustrate a mobility barrier because they:

options.A: Prevent straightforward expansion of scope within finance
options.B: Remove rivalry by forcing all fintechs to coordinate
options.C: Eliminate buyer power by creating universal switching costs
options.D: Collapse substitutes by creating stronger network effects

questions.stem: In strategic group logic, the fiercest rivalry is typically:

options.A: Only between suppliers who sell inputs to all firms
options.B: Within the same group where offerings and economics overlap
options.C: Across distant groups where offerings are structurally distinct
options.D: Only between complements that jointly raise demand

questions.stem: A firm’s attempt to “move upmarket” fails most often because:

options.A: Substitutes vanish and consumers lose alternative options
options.B: Entry threat collapses and capital markets become irrelevant
options.C: Activity systems and brand signals are slow to rebuild
options.D: Buyer power disappears and customers stop comparing prices

questions.stem: The most precise relationship between mobility barriers and entry barriers is:

options.A: Mobility and entry always move in the same direction
options.B: Mobility matters only when entry threat is zero
options.C: Mobility disappears when substitutes increase rapidly
options.D: Mobility can be high even when entry is moderate

questions.stem: A strategic group map is least useful when:

options.A: Firms are nearly identical and compete only on price
options.B: Firms differ widely in scope, service, and cost structure
options.C: Product differentiation creates stable clusters of rivals
options.D: Mobility barriers block rapid repositioning attempts

questions.stem: For social platforms, “algorithmic distribution” often acts like:

options.A: An ecological factor because it changes carbon intensity
options.B: A mobility barrier because it is path-dependent and cumulative
options.C: A substitute because it replaces user attention entirely
options.D: A supplier because it is purchased as an external input

questions.stem: TikTok’s forced restructuring is likely to alter which group boundary most?

options.A: “High capex” vs “low capex” heavy manufacturing firms
options.B: “Old economy” vs “new economy” firms in general
options.C: “National-security compliant” vs “cross-border controlled” platforms
options.D: “Premium priced” vs “low priced” consumer goods sellers

questions.stem: In group terms, “mobility barriers” are closest to:

options.A: Marketing slogans that can be changed in a week
options.B: Buyer preferences that shift randomly without drivers
options.C: One-time shocks that disappear without lasting effects
options.D: Structural walls that make imitation costly and slow

questions.stem: The key error students make with group maps is:

options.A: Using too many dimensions and losing interpretability
options.B: Using too few dimensions and making it too simple
options.C: Treating groups as moral categories of “good” and “bad”
options.D: Treating groups as identical to PESTEL categories

questions.stem: “Premium trust” in airlines is best treated as what kind of asset in mobility terms?

options.A: A political mandate that automatically ensures demand
options.B: Reputation capital that is slow to build and easy to lose
options.C: A commodity input that can be purchased instantly
options.D: A substitute that replaces safety engineering entirely

questions.stem: Which is the best example of “mobility barrier via regulation”?

options.A: A substitute product solving the job differently
options.B: A buyer negotiating discounts via bulk purchases
options.C: A licence requirement that restricts product scope expansion
options.D: A new entrant copying a UI and buying ads cheaply

questions.stem: Strategic groups connect to Five Forces because:

options.A: Forces become identical once the industry boundary is set
options.B: Forces disappear when groups are mapped correctly
options.C: Forces are purely internal capabilities, not external structure
options.D: Forces differ in intensity by group location and economics

questions.stem: A “low-cost” group is protected most by:

options.A: Cost system discipline and activity fit, not single features
options.B: A single ad campaign that changes brand perception quickly
options.C: A one-off discount that permanently locks-in customers
options.D: A legal decree that prevents consumers from switching

questions.stem: If a firm tries to span two distant groups, the biggest structural danger is:

options.A: Lower supplier power that makes inputs cheaper over time
options.B: Internal contradictions that destroy both cost and differentiation
options.C: Lower entry barriers that suddenly invite thousands of entrants
options.D: Lower substitutes that make demand perfectly inelastic

questions.stem: A “strategic group” is best defined as:

options.A: Firms facing identical macro shocks in the general environment
options.B: Firms that share the same suppliers and the same buyers
options.C: Firms with similar strategies competing on similar dimensions
options.D: Firms with identical missions and identical internal cultures

questions.stem: A group boundary becomes a “barrier” when:

options.A: Moving across it requires only messaging and rebranding
options.B: Moving across it requires only a short-term discount
options.C: Moving across it requires only hiring a new CEO
options.D: Moving across it requires large, irreversible commitments

questions.stem: The sharpest reason strategic groups matter for students is:

options.A: They prevent naïve “one-industry one-strategy” thinking
options.B: They eliminate the need for industry structure analysis
options.C: They remove the need for market definition discipline
options.D: They substitute for quantitative performance measures

questions.stem: A common “category error” is to treat DMA as mainly technological because it affects app design. Why is that wrong?

options.A: The driver is ecological scarcity, not platform governance
options.B: The initiating driver is legal constraint, not innovation
options.C: The driver is inflation transmission, not rules or mandates
options.D: The driver is demographic change, not institutional policy

questions.stem: If a shock increases fixed compliance costs, the most Porteresque prediction is:

options.A: Supplier power collapses because suppliers hate paperwork
options.B: Rivalry disappears because firms become more ethical
options.C: Entry threat falls when fixed costs deter small challengers
options.D: Entry threat rises because compliance is a demand stimulator

questions.stem: A strategy memo that lists “inflation, AI, ESG, geopolitics” but offers no mechanisms is failing at:

options.A: Calculating WACC precisely for each business segment
options.B: Writing a mission statement with emotionally resonant verbs
options.C: Choosing a new organisational structure for ambidexterity
options.D: Translating environment into causal impacts on profitability

questions.stem: A firm facing Red Sea shipping disruption should not conclude automatically that:

options.A: Higher freight rates imply higher pricing power for the firm
options.B: Higher freight rates can raise costs and shift demand
options.C: Rerouting can increase lead times and working capital
options.D: Risk can raise insurance costs and supplier leverage

questions.stem: TikTok’s restructuring risk is analytically closest to which Five Forces channel?

options.A: Rivalry decline reshaping the number of active platforms
options.B: Regulatory constraint reshaping entry, conduct, and capture
options.C: Supplier concentration reshaping semiconductor input prices
options.D: Substitute pressure reshaping demand away from short video

questions.stem: A subtle but crucial distinction: “buyers are powerful” means they can:

options.A: Force substitutes to disappear from adjacent industries
options.B: Force entry barriers to rise through scale economies
options.C: Force price concessions by credible switching or volume
options.D: Force suppliers to merge and reduce input variety

questions.stem: The cleanest indicator that an industry is in “shakeout/maturity” is:

options.A: Growth explodes and new entrants flood in monthly
options.B: Product meaning shifts and consumers adopt new norms
options.C: Regulation disappears and compliance costs fall sharply
options.D: Growth slows and consolidation rises as weaker firms exit

questions.stem: Google’s monopoly remedies debate is best used to teach:

options.A: How rule changes can rewire entry barriers and distribution
options.B: How culture change alone can eliminate competitive forces
options.C: How inflation reduces substitutes by lowering innovation
options.D: How demographics automatically raise switching costs

questions.stem: In external analysis, “industry attractiveness” is primarily about:

options.A: The firm’s mission statement and ethical commitments
options.B: Structural profit potential, not a firm’s current share
options.C: A firm’s internal capabilities and VRIO resources
options.D: The CEO’s charisma and leadership narrative skill

questions.stem: A correct reading of “value capture is a power game” is:

options.A: Complements always capture value regardless of contracts
options.B: Buyers never capture value because they do not produce
options.C: Bargaining power decides who keeps surplus, not who creates it
options.D: Innovation always captures value regardless of structure

questions.stem: A “strategic group” analysis adds most when Five Forces says:

options.A: “Low rivalry” overall, and all firms earn identical returns
options.B: “High entry” overall, and no firm survives past a year
options.C: “High substitutes” overall, and demand is already collapsing
options.D: “Moderate” overall, but profit differences persist across clusters

questions.stem: The best one-line definition of “mobility barrier” is:

options.A: Costly constraint preventing repositioning across strategic clusters
options.B: Costly constraint preventing any new entrant from entering
options.C: Costly constraint preventing substitutes from being invented
options.D: Costly constraint preventing buyers from negotiating price

questions.stem: A firm that copies a market leader under uncertainty is showing:

options.A: Complementarity as a demand-expansion mechanism
options.B: Mimetic isomorphism as a legitimacy-seeking response
options.C: Predatory pricing as a deliberate rivalry escalator
options.D: Perfect competition as a structural inevitability

questions.stem: Reddit’s IPO is most useful here to ask: “What changed structurally?” The most defensible answer is:

options.A: Supplier power vanished because the ticker symbol is new
options.B: Substitutes declined because users prefer listed companies
options.C: Governance and disclosure pressures changed, not the industry map
options.D: Entry barriers collapsed because IPOs create public liquidity

questions.stem: A firm hit by Paytm-like regulatory constraints should first test:

options.A: Whether substitutes vanished because regulation became strict
options.B: Whether suppliers became fragmented because audits increased
options.C: Whether rivalry fell because compliance teams are expensive
options.D: Whether its “industry definition” must narrow to allowed scope

questions.stem: In PESTEL, the most precise reason “unemployment is low” matters is:

options.A: Wage pressure rises, shifting costs and bargaining dynamics
options.B: Entry barriers rise because firms cannot hire CEOs
options.C: Substitutes vanish because labour becomes scarce
options.D: Rivalry disappears because demand becomes predictable

questions.stem: Which statement is most accurate about “externalities” in ecological analysis?

options.A: Costs not priced in always increase complements immediately
options.B: Costs not priced in can later return as regulation or backlash
options.C: Costs not priced in always vanish because markets are efficient
options.D: Costs not priced in always reduce rivalry across all industries

questions.stem: A firm claims “we will beat rivals by working harder.” The best Session 8 critique is:

options.A: Effort eliminates substitutes because customers admire hustle
options.B: Effort lowers interest rates by improving investor sentiment
options.C: Structure and power can dominate effort; analyse constraints first
options.D: Effort guarantees monopoly power if culture is strong

questions.stem: The most rigorous use of “strategic groups” in a case write-up is to:

options.A: List every competitor alphabetically with market shares
options.B: Replace Five Forces with a colourful diagram and quotes
options.C: Provide mission statements and values of each firm
options.D: Specify axes, justify clusters, and name mobility barriers

questions.stem: A robust five-forces memo should avoid:

options.A: Treating “competition” as rivalry only, ignoring other forces
options.B: Defining buyers as buyers, not confusing them with users
options.C: Describing substitutes as different solutions to the same need
options.D: Stating which force is strongest and why, with evidence

questions.stem: When students confuse complements and substitutes, the telltale sign is they:

options.A: Treat “rivalry” as always being low when growth is high
options.B: Treat “charging stations” as replacing EVs rather than enabling
options.C: Treat “new entrants” as solving the same job differently
options.D: Treat “buyers” as always being the end consumer

questions.stem: A correct interpretation of “price taker” is:

options.A: Firm can collude costlessly because rivals are fragmented
options.B: Firm can block entry because switching costs are infinite
options.C: Firm faces elastic demand at market price and lacks power
options.D: Firm can set price above marginal cost without losing volume

questions.stem: If you must write one sentence that unifies Session 8, the best is:

options.A: Decide how you compete before defining where you compete
options.B: Ignore structure because leadership can override all forces
options.C: Ignore environment because purpose guarantees profitability
options.D: Define where you compete before deciding how you compete
